info.bio:
Little Richard, nombre artístico de Richard Wayne Penniman, (Macon, Georgia; 5 de diciembre de 1932-Tullahoma, Tennessee; 9 de mayo de 2020)​ fue un cantante y pianista estadounidense de rock and roll. Fue considerado uno de los pioneros más influyentes e importantes de la historia del rock.

Es muy difícil que cuando se diga rock and roll alguien no piense en los gritos de Little Richard. Quizás ningún otro artista, exceptuando a Elvis, tuvo un papel tan importante en la construcción de los cimientos del rock and roll.

scenes.name: Soul y R&B
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 1 de enero de 1966 el Top 3 estadounidense lo formaban «The Sound of Silence», «We Can Work It Out» y el «I Got You (I Feel Good)» de James Brown: discos futuristas los tres. A finales de mes Otis Redding se acercaba al Top 10 británico con su versión de «My Girl» de los Temptations.

scenes.name: Rhythm and blues
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: En los cuarenta, los combos de jump como el Tympany Five de Louis Jordan sustituyeron a las big bands: baile, ritmo, scat, solo de saxo. Gente que trabajaba duro todo el día necesitaba música fuerte y con alma: un grito sincero, un saxo, una guitarra rockera. Su «misma vulgaridad», dice LeRoi Jones, aseguraba su conexión con la vida de la gente, y esa vulgaridad fue el ingrediente principal del funk. Despreciado por los intelectuales como mal jazz, el R&B dio a Chuck Berry, Little Richard y Bo Diddley, inspiró el rock and roll y la invasión británica, y en el chitlin circuit fue el útero del funk. Con Live at the Apollo de James Brown (1962, disco de oro) el R&B se hizo mayor; de él salieron Ray Charles, Brown y Aretha Franklin.
scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B

scenes.name: Jimi Hendrix
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La historia de Hendrix se ha escrito desde el rock (blanco) y no desde el funk (negro), pese a su herencia, su formación y sus bandas negras. Criado en el Seattle multirracial, en el ejército descubrió el blues de Nashville y el sonido de Memphis, tocó con Little Richard, aprendió de Albert King y fue guitarrista de los Isley Brothers en Harlem, protegido por la red social negra. Chas Chandler lo llevó a Londres; en Monterey (1967) nació una nueva era. «If 6 Was 9» («voy a ondear mi bandera de bicho raro») articulaba los choques culturales que él provocaba. En Woodstock tocó con una banda multirracial de seis músicos con percusionistas afrolatinos que el ingeniero borró de la mezcla; luego formó la Band of Gypsys con Buddy Miles y Billy Cox, grabó con Lightnin’ Rod de los Last Poets y quiso tocar para los Panteras. Murió en 1970, un día después de tocar con War. No tuvo música de baile ni sitio en la radio negra, pero su huella en Miles, Prince, Bootsy, Clinton, Eddie Hazel, los Isley o Stevie Wonder fue profunda.
scenes.family: Funk psicodélico y black rock: Sly, Hendrix

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

They performed like animals, and added another level of provocation: clothes and facial make-up that were obscene. Esquerita and Little Richard invented decadence-rock. Little Richard's frenzied songs of the time would remain the most hysterical specimens of rock'n'roll until punk-rock: Tutti Frutti (1955), Long Tall Sally (1956),…

podcast.title: Career Low Point (1953)
podcast.body: Following his arrest and being dropped by two record labels (RCA and Peacock), the split of his band The Tempo Toppers, and the recent death of his father, Richard was at a very low point in his career, unable to live in his hometown. "Things seemed pretty low."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Explosion into Public Consciousness (1955)
podcast.body: Little Richard, along with Elvis, Chuck Berry, Bo Diddly, and Bill Haley, exploded into public consciousness in 1955, marking the birth of rock and roll. "they all exploded into public consciousness that year, 1955, the birth of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sustained Rock and Roll Success (1956)
podcast.body: By late 1956, Little Richard remained a prominent artist, specifically a black R&B star, who consistently achieved actual rock and roll hits that climbed to respectable positions on the charts. This contrasted with the fading success of many white rockabilly acts. "If we're talking about actual rock and roll hits rising to decent positions in the charts, by late 1956 you're looking at acts like Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Fat Stomano with only Elvis left of the rock-a-billy's."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Crisis of Faith and Music Hiatus (1957)
podcast.body: Little Richard, one of the first rock and roll stars and one of the first black rock and roll stars, experienced a crisis of faith in 1957 while in the middle of a tour of Australia. This crisis was triggered by dreaming of his own damnation, which he attributed largely to his closeted gayness. He subsequently quit the music business for five years, and after returning, he never truly regained the level of success and prominence he had enjoyed in the mid-1950s. "dreaming of his own damn nation, much of which had to do with his closeted gainess."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Featured in Rock and Roll Film (1957)
podcast.body: Little Richard was featured in the 1957 Alan Fried film, "Mr. Rock and Roll," alongside other rock and roll and R&B stars. This film also notably included Lionel Hampton, the only jazz musician in the lineup, highlighting the cross-genre recognition of pioneers. "You can see him in the 1957 Alan Fried film, Mr. Rock and Roll, playing his vibraphone, as the only jazz musician in a film which otherwise features Little Richard, Clyde McFatter, and other rock and Darwin-based stars at the time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 1: "Flying Home", Benny Goodman, Charlie Christian, and Lionel Hampton

podcast.title: Religious Conversion Experience (October 1957)
podcast.body: While on a tour of Australia in October 1957, Little Richard experienced a profound religious awakening after seeing a plane engine glowing red, convincing him of angels, and then witnessing Russia's Sputnik satellite pass low over Australia like a "fireball," which he interpreted as a divine sign to abandon his sinful life for religion. To prove his sincerity, he threw all his rings into the ocean and abruptly canceled the remaining ten days of the tour to return to the US. "He decided this was a sign, and he was being told by God he needed to give up his life of sin and devote himself to religion."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Comeback Spurred by Sam Cooke (1962)
podcast.body: During his October 1962 UK tour, which he intended to be gospel-focused, Little Richard was confronted by an audience expecting rock and roll. His competitive nature was ignited by Sam Cooke's "incendiary performance" of "Twistin' the Night Away," serving as the "final straw" that propelled Richard back to performing rock and roll. "Cook was at the height of his success at this point and he was an astonishing live performer and so when he went out on stage and closed the first half including an insendiary performance of twist in the night away that left the audience applauding through the intermission Richard knew he had to up his game."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mentoring The Beatles in Hamburg (1962)
podcast.body: After his successful UK tour, Little Richard spent two months in Hamburg hanging out and performing in clubs with The Beatles, a local Mersey's side band. During this time, he personally taught their bass player, Paul McCartney, how to make his distinctive "woo" sounds when singing. "He then went to Hamburg with that group and spent two months hanging out with them and performing it in the same kinds of clubs and teaching their bass player how he made his wool sounds when singing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Officiated Bruce Willis and Demi Moore's Wedding (1987)
podcast.body: In November 1987, Little Richard, who was an ordained minister, officiated the marriage of actors Bruce Willis and Demi Moore. His role as the officiating pastor made the ceremony legally binding. "the officiating pastor was Little Richard. He was an ordained minister, so was illegal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Performance in Golden Wheelchair (2013)
podcast.body: Little Richard retired from live performing a few years ago due to disabilities exacerbated by decades of strenuous stage shows. His last public performance was in 2013 in Las Vegas, where, ever the showman, he appeared in a wheelchair that was custom-made to look like a "golden throne." "His last public performance was in 2013, in Las Vegas, and he was in a wheelchair, but, because he's little Richard, the wheelchair was made to look like a golden throne."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Death Marked (2020)
podcast.body: The death of Little Richard was marked as a significant event in music history, acknowledging his profound importance to 20th-century music. His work had previously been covered in episodes on "Tutti Frutti" and "Keep a Knockin'." "Without Little Richard, none of the music we're covering in this podcast after 1955 would be the same, and this podcast would not exist."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: "Tutti Frutti" Publishing Deal
podcast.body: The publishing rights for "Tutti Frutti" were owned by a company belonging to Art Rupe, the owner of Specialty Records. This company licensed the song to Specialty for half the normal mechanical licensing rate (one cent per record instead of two cents), a common practice with independent labels that Richard later resented. "This sort of cross collateralisation was common with independent labels at the time, but it still wrankled to Richard when he figured it out."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: 50s Importance Debate
podcast.body: Little Richard is considered one of the three most important artists of the 1950s, alongside Elvis Presley and Chuck Berry. It's argued that no one else can make a good case for being as important as these three. "We can argue about which of Elvis, Tukberi or Little Richard was the most important artist of the 50s, but I don't think you can make a good argument that anyone other than one of those three was."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Abuse and Injury from Don Roby
podcast.body: Don Roby, owner of Peacock Records, was reportedly disrespectful and treated his artists poorly. Richard openly criticized Roby, who retaliated by beating Richard so severely that it caused a hernia, which hurt for years and required an operation. "Roby responded, by beating Richard up so badly that he got a hernia, which hurt for years and necessitated an operation."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Adopting the Pompadour and Name
podcast.body: While touring with Bee Brown and his Orchestra, Richard grew his hair into the huge pompadour that would become his trademark. It was also during this period that he acquired the name Little Richard. "It was while he was touring with that band, that he grew his hair into the huge pumpador that would later become a trademark, and he also got the name Little Richard."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: African American Originator of Rock
podcast.body: Ice-T frequently noted that rock music stemmed from African American artists, including Little Richard. "Ice Tea was always quick to point out that rock originated with African American artists like Chuck Berry and Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Agent Clint Brantley and "Ghosting" Gigs
podcast.body: Due to Little Richard's rapidly increasing success and bookings into larger halls, his agent, Clint Brantley, devised a plan for James Brown and The Flames to "ghost" the remaining smaller gigs Richard was contracted for. Since few people knew what Richard looked like, Brown and The Flames pretended to be Little Richard and The Upsetters, performing his material and their own, with Brown adopting Richard's introduction, "please welcome the hardest working man in show business today." "No one knew what Richard looked like, so the agent got Brown and The Flames to pretend to be Little Richard and The Upsetters, and tore playing the gigs that Richard had been booked into."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 39: "Please Please Please" by James Brown and the Famous Flames

podcast.title: Agile and Rebellious Roots of Rock
podcast.body: Little Richard embodies the early, youthful, fun, agile, and rebellious spirit of rock music, providing a contrast to the intellectual and complex progressive rock that emerged later. "La raíces del roque, pues como Virhali o como Chuck Berry o como Little Richard eran movimientos muy jóvenes, muy divertidos, muy ágiles, muy rebeldes."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Qué es el NO WAVE. Es mucho más que música

podcast.title: Backstage Anecdote at Paramount (Year not specified)
podcast.body: During a residency at the Brooklyn Paramount on an Alan Fried show, Little Richard and Larry Williams were discovered engaged in a threesome with Richard's girlfriend when The Crickets entered their dressing room. "Richard and Williams engaged in a threesome with Richard's girlfriend."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Moral Beliefs Distribution
podcast.body: During various religious periods in his career, Little Richard's rider specified that he be allowed to distribute souvenir books summarizing his moral beliefs free of charge to the audience, reflecting his strong spiritual convictions at the time. "His writer specified that he'd be able to distribute free of charge souvenir books that summarized Little Richard's moral beliefs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bumps Blackwell Conflict with Art Rupe
podcast.body: During the recording of "Rip It Up," Bumps Blackwell nearly got fired by Art Rupe for unilaterally changing the arrangement to a drum pattern instead of the pre-approved piano triplets, a decision Rupe only tolerated after the record became a massive hit. "Rube had nearly fired black well over that, and only relented when the record became a massive hit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Characteristic Vocal and Guitar Style (1950s)
podcast.body: Little Richard exemplified the structural simplicity prevalent in early rock, characterized by his acute, baritone voice. His music featured a continuous interplay where his high-pitched vocals alternated with an equally acute electric guitar, the latter serving to complement or continue the melody when he stopped singing. "Tenemos esas voces agudas baritonas como podía tener Lita El Richard en la que marca continuamente todo el ritmo con su voz."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cómo LED ZEPPELIN inventó el ROCK MODERNO

podcast.title: Childhood and Disability
podcast.body: Born Richard Penniman, he was the third of twelve children and known for causing trouble, including practical jokes with his own feces. As a child, he was terribly bullied due to physical disabilities: one leg significantly shorter than the other, a disproportionately large head, and different sized eyes. He also faced homophobic abuse from a young age due to his "vaguely mincing" gait. "He was also terribly bullied as a child, because he was disabled."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Complex Sexuality and Gender Identity
podcast.body: Little Richard's sexuality and gender identity are described as complex, as he defined himself as gay at various times but also had relationships with women. His autobiography contains passages where he wished he had been born a woman, suggesting that had he been born later, he might have identified as a bisexual trans woman. "He has at various times defined himself as gay, but he has also had relationships with women, and from reading his autobiography, there are so many passages where he talks about wishing he had been born a woman, that it may well be, that had he been born 50 years later, he would have defined himself as a bisexual trans woman, rather than a gay man."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Conflict and Identity Struggles
podcast.body: Little Richard was deeply conflicted throughout his life, grappling with his attraction to both men and women, his love for rock and roll versus his profound religious beliefs, his enjoyment of indulgent food, drink, and drugs, and an uncertainty about his own gender identity. "Richard had always been deeply conflicted about, well, about everything really."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Contract Buyout for $600
podcast.body: Specialty Records, after hearing Richard's demo, made an agreement with Don Roby of Peacock Records to buy out Richard's contract for $600. It was implied that Roby was so eager to be rid of Richard that he might have paid Specialty to take him. "Blackwell and Roup made an agreement with Don Roby to buy out his contract for $600."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Contractual Dispute with Specialty Records
podcast.body: According to John Mariscalco, Little Richard's conversion in 1957 might have been partially motivated by a desire to break his contract with Specialty Records, which only paid him half a cent per record and allowed termination only upon his death or an "act of God"; Richard allegedly aimed to claim his religious awakening as an "act of God" to escape the unfavorable terms. "Richard's contract with specialty was only paying him half a cent per record sold, which he considered far too low, and the wording of the contract only let him end it on either his own death or an act of God."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Discovery of "Tutti Frutti" at the Dew Drop Inn
podcast.body: During a break from an unproductive Specialty Records session, Little Richard went to the Dew Drop Inn. There, he performed "Tutti Frutti" on the piano for an audience, instantly impressing Bumps Blackwell with its hit potential despite its sexually explicit original lyrics. "The dude drop in had a piano, and it had an audience that Little Richard could show off in front of."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dramatic Stage Persona and Antics
podcast.body: Little Richard's 1962 British tour was marked by his increasingly wild and frantic stage performances, reflecting five years of pent-up rock and roll energy. He frequently threw off clothes into the audience, dressed in just a bathrobe on his knees, jumped on the piano, and famously faked his own death mid-song before springing up to sing "Tutti Frutti," all designed to captivate and energize the audience. "Many shows he'd pull off most of his clothes and throw them into the audience and he got dressed in just a bathrobe on his knees."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Drip-Feeding Recordings
podcast.body: Specialty Records had a strategy of "drip-feeding" Little Richard's recordings to the public, implying they had a limited number of unreleased tracks. This strategy was disrupted when Bumps Blackwell forced their hand with a counter-release. "A blow for them, given that they were trying to drip-feed the public what few Little Richard recordings they had left."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Early Performance Career (Age 14)
podcast.body: At the age of fourteen, Richard left school to pursue a performing career. He began by touring with a snake oil salesman named Doc Hudson, singing the non-religious song "Caldonia" by Louis Jordan. "At the age of fourteen he decided to leave school and become a performer."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Music
podcast.body: Little Richard's music was directly associated with the rock and roll sound of the 1950s and early 60s, which was a direct descendant of 12-bar blues. This music was characterized by clean, clear guitar sounds and mostly clean lyrics, often intended for kids and played on radio stations appealing to teenagers. "the rock and roll sound became associated and intertwined with the music of the 1950s and early 60s, Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
podcast.body: Little Richard was an early pioneer of rock and roll, recognized as one of the "piano heroes" who led the genre before the electric guitar became dominant. These pioneers were known for their energetic piano playing, contributing to the "honkin rhythm" that characterized early rock and roll, which evolved from rhythm and blues combos. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Pioneer
podcast.body: Little Richard was a key figure in the 1950s when R&B and other genres combined to create rock and roll. "Rock and Roll begins in the 1950s when R&B and several other genres merge, thanks to Elvis, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Pioneer
podcast.body: Little Richard's music was directly associated with the rock and roll sound of the 1950s and early 60s, which was a direct descendant of 12-bar blues. This music was characterized by clean, clear guitar sounds and mostly clean lyrics, often intended for kids and played on radio stations appealing to teenagers. "the rock and roll sound became associated and intertwined with the music of the 1950s and early 60s, Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Pioneer
podcast.body: Little Richard is cited as one of the major stars of the early rock and roll era, a romantic figure of legend who is well-documented in many books, in contrast to other important but lesser-known artists of the period. "While you won't find much out there on a lot of truly important artists, you can find out enough about Elvis and Ray Charles and Johnny Cash and Little Richard and Chuck Berry in the rest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Star
podcast.body: Little Richard is cited as one of the major stars of the early rock and roll era, a romantic figure of legend who is well-documented in many books, in contrast to other important but lesser-known artists of the period. "While you won't find much out there on a lot of truly important artists, you can find out enough about Elvis and Ray Charles and Johnny Cash and Little Richard and Chuck Berry in the rest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Enduring Live Performer (1960s-2010s)
podcast.body: While his recording career faltered, Little Richard remained a formidable live performer, touring for 50 years and playing his classic hits from 1955-1957. These decades of performing were interspersed with periodic bouts of remorse where he would temporarily abandon rock and roll for evangelism, only to be drawn back by "the lure of material success and audience response." "They hadn't though, killed him as a live performer, and he would spend the next 50 years touring, playing the hits he had recorded, during that classic period from 1955 through 1957..."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Female Impersonation
podcast.body: Richard's performances as a female impersonator began when he had to cover for a sick woman in one of the touring shows, quickly donning her costume. He soon found himself performing in shows predominantly featuring drag performers for largely gay crowds. "It was while he was performing in these shows that he met the first of his two biggest influences."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Flamboyance and Influence
podcast.body: Despite performing as a Black and gay artist in the US South in the 1950s, Little Richard's flamboyance, energy, and music had a massive effect across rock and roll. His influence extended to artists like The Beatles, James Brown, David Bowie, and even Lemmy of Motorhead, reverberating through the entire genre. "His flamboyance, his energy, and his music reverberated through all of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fundamentalist Christian Beliefs
podcast.body: Little Richard is a very religious man, holding a specific variety of fundamentalist Christianity that condemns any sexuality or gender identity other than monogamous cis heterosexual as evil and sinful. He deeply believes this and has often tried to live his life by these beliefs. "Little Richard is also a very, very religious man, and a believer in a specific variety of fundamentalist Christianity that believes that any kind of sexuality or gender identity, other than monogamous cis heterosexual, is evil and sinful and the work of the devil."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Giant of Rock Music
podcast.body: Little Richard is recognized as one of the significant figures in the broader landscape of rock music. "Where would we be with a bow diddly and little Richard and Jimmy Hendrix?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: High School Ambition
podcast.body: In high school, Dylan's ambition, as recorded in his yearbook, was to join Little Richard's band. "his ambition, as quoted in his high school yearbook, was to join Little Richard's band."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Hiring an Imposter for Low-Class Gigs
podcast.body: As Richard became a huge star, he had concert bookings in second-rate clubs that conflicted with his need to be in Hollywood to promote his new record. To avoid a reputation for missing gigs, he hired an imposter, James Brown, to perform as "Little Richard" at these lower-tier venues. "So while Richard went off to promote his record, another young singer from Georgia, with a pompadour and a gospel feel, was being introduced with the phrase, Ladies and Gentlemen, the hardest working man in show business today, little Richard."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Impact on Rock's Momentum
podcast.body: Little Richard is cited as one of the key figures whose emergence, alongside Elvis and Jerry Lee Lewis, made rock music unstoppable. Despite widespread criticism, record burnings, and attempts by authorities to crack down on the genre, rock solidified its presence in music following his rise. "None of this actually slowed anything down, of course. We got Elvis, then Little Richard, then Jerry Lee Lewis. And then after that, the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impressed Johnny Otis
podcast.body: Johnny Otis was highly impressed by Richard's live performance, describing him as "outrageous," "good looking and very effeminate," with a big pompadour. Otis likened his singing to Dinah Washington and was particularly amused when Richard, after proclaiming himself "King of the Blues," added "and the Queen too." "Otis said, I see this outrageous person, good looking and very effeminate, with a big pumpador."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influences from Billy Wright
podcast.body: Billy Wright, a blues star from 1949-1951, greatly influenced Richard. Wright was a female impersonator with a pompadour and was one of the first blues singers to use gospel-inspired vocalizations ("panorasms"). Richard imitated Wright's style, including using "pancake 31" make-up on stage, a practice he continued throughout his career. "Richard became something of a bellywright wannabe and started incorporating parts of right style into his performances."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Inspiration for James Brown
podcast.body: Little Richard's musical style and performance were a direct inspiration for James Brown, influencing the direction of soul and funk music. "he was the inspiration for James Brown."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Internal Conflict with Sexuality
podcast.body: Little Richard's relationship with his sexuality was complex, marked by a constant internal war. He sometimes reveled in it, showcasing his flamboyant personality, but at other times experienced periods of self-loathing, indicating a conflicted personal journey. "That Little Richard was always at war with his sexuality, sometimes exalting in it, sometimes descending into self-loathing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Learning Piano from Escarito
podcast.body: Richard was solely a singer until he met Escarito, another gay, black R&B singer, who also played piano. Richard consistently stated that Escarito taught him to play the piano, claiming his own piano style was a copy of Escarito's and that Escarito was a better player. "Richard soon learned to play piano, and he was seen by Johnny Otis, who was impressed."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Legal Troubles and Exile from Macon
podcast.body: Around the time he was dropped by Peacock Records, Richard was arrested for "lewd conduct," which amounted to consensual voyeurism. This incident forced him to move away from his hometown of Macon, Georgia. "He was also, around the same time, made to move away from Macon, Georgia, where he lived, after being arrested for lured conduct."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Lyrical Embarrassment for "Tutti Frutti"
podcast.body: When Dorothy LaBostrie was tasked with rewriting the explicit lyrics of "Tutti Frutti" to be broadcastable, Richard, despite his usual flamboyance, became embarrassed to sing the song in front of the "innocent looking young woman." He eventually agreed to sing it, but only if he was turned to face the wall. "Richard, not normally a man overly known for his modesty, became embarrassed at singing his song to the young woman."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Lyrical Style Comparison
podcast.body: The "carefree gibberish lyrics" found in Gene Vincent's "Be-Bop-A-Lula" are stylistically compared to those of Little Richard, noting their contribution to the overall sound and impact of the record. "It still has that strange morbidity that the Elvis track had, but combined with carefree gibberish lyrics in the style of Little Richard."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Massive Influence on James Brown
podcast.body: Little Richard had a profound influence on James Brown, to the point that Brown initially acted as a tribute act for him. Both artists, hailing from Georgia, shared significant inspiration from Louis Jordan and church music. "Brown was massively influenced by Little Richard, to the extent that he was essentially a Little Richard tribute act early on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 39: "Please Please Please" by James Brown and the Famous Flames

podcast.title: Musical Comparison to George Jones
podcast.body: George Jones's 1959 hit "White Lightning" was described as having a sound that evoked Little Richard, further highlighting its early rock and roll characteristics. "I hear a little bit of Richard in there too."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Persistent Demo Submissions to Specialty Records
podcast.body: Lloyd Price suggested Richard send a demo tape to Specialty Records. The tape lay unheard for months until Richard's constant pestering finally prompted Bumps Blackwell, A&R at Specialty, to listen to it. "The tape lay on-listened at specialty for months, and it was only because of Richard's constant pestering for them to listen to it, that Bump's Blackwell, who was then in charge of A&R at specialty, eventually got round to listening to it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Piano Style Influence
podcast.body: Young Robert Zimmerman (Bob Dylan) taught himself to play rudimentary piano in the distinctive style of Little Richard. "He taught himself to play Rudimentri Piano in a little Richard style"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Pioneer Black Crossover Artist
podcast.body: Little Richard was the first Black artist to successfully cross over, appealing to both Black and white audiences and effectively breaking the color barrier. His shows attracted people of all races, significantly contributing to cultural change in the segregated 1950s. "Little Richard was the first black artist to cross over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneer of Flamboyance
podcast.body: Little Richard is noted as the most flamboyant member of rock's first generation, known for his distinctive hair, costumes, makeup, wild performances, and "unclear sexuality," which contributed to a style that influenced later artists. "Little Richard, the most flamboyant member of Rock's First Generation. He had the hair, the costumes, the makeup, the wild performances, and the... Well, let's just call it unclear sexuality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Popular with British Teenagers
podcast.body: British teenagers were drawn to his American records, which were vastly different from the output of the British commercial rock and roll industry during that period. "British teenagers were instead listening to American records by Buddy Holly or Little Richard, the Avley Brothers or Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Post-Conversion Lifestyle Changes
podcast.body: After his conversion, Little Richard drastically altered his lifestyle: he became an evangelist, studied for the ministry, married a woman (though they later divorced due to sexual incompatibility), ceased drinking alcohol, taking drugs, and even consuming coffee, and adopted a strict vegetarian diet cooked solely in vegetable oil. "He changed his whole lifestyle. He married a woman, although they were later divorced as, among other things, they weren't sexually compatible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Recording Career Decline in the 1960s
podcast.body: His five-year absence from rock and roll music severely damaged Little Richard's career as a recording artist, leading to a string of chart failures throughout the rest of the 1960s, despite some recordings being as good as his 1950s heyday material. "his 5 years away from rock and roll music had killed his career as a recording artist."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rock's First Openly Gay Rock Star
podcast.body: Little Richard is argued to be rock's first openly gay rock star, or at least bisexual with strong gay leanings. He openly embraced effeminate mannerisms, wore makeup, engaged in "rough trade," and famously declared, "Elvis may have been the king of rock and roll, but I and the queen." "you can make an argument that he was Rock's first openly gay rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Self-Proclaimed Title
podcast.body: Little Richard famously described himself as "the king and queen of rock and roll." "the force of nature, who described himself as the king and queen of rock and roll."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Self-Written Hit (1950s)
podcast.body: Little Richard distinguished his recording career from the prevalent "song for hire" model of the 1950s by writing "Tutti Frutti" himself, with lyric editor Dorothy LaBostrie providing a "sanitizing assist" to the lyrics. "Little Richard had written it himself with a sanitizing assist from lyrics editor Dorothy LaBostry."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Seminary Expulsion and Arrest
podcast.body: His internal conflict between sexuality and religion continued to torment him, leading to him dropping out of the seminary after propositioning another male student and later being arrested in a public toilet. "He dropped out of the seminary after propositioning another male student, and he was arrested in a public toilet."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Seventh-day Adventist Faith
podcast.body: Little Richard was a deeply religious believer in the Seventh-day Adventist Church, which held strict views condemning same-sex attraction, trans identities, and secular music as "the work of the devil," advocating for a vegetarian and kosher diet, and prohibiting all drugs, including caffeine. "He was also deeply, deeply religious, and a believer in the seventh day Adventist Church, which believed that same sex attraction, trans identities, and secular music would the work of the devil and that one should keep a vegetarian and kosher diet and avoid old drugs even caffeine."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Significant Influence on Richie Valens
podcast.body: Little Richard's R&B music was a major source of inspiration and interest for Richie Valens during his formative years in high school. Valens was particularly drawn to Little Richard's style, alongside that of Larry Williams, both artists known for recording on Specialty Records. "Valens' big interest in school was music, especially R&B, and especially the music of Little Richard and Larry Williams, and other people who had recorded for specialty records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Swinging Between Secular and Divine
podcast.body: Richard's life has been characterized by wild swings between embodying the "sex and drugs and rock and roll" lifestyle and renouncing it to embrace his fundamentalist Christian beliefs, where he claims homosexuality, bisexuality, and being trans are works of the literal devil. As of 2017, he had once again renounced rock and roll and same-sex relationships. "He has swung wildly between being almost the literal embodiment of the phrase sex and drugs and rock and roll, and being a creature who claims that homosexuality, bisexuality, and being trans are all works of the literal devil, several times he's gone from one to the other."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: True Original in Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Little Richard is considered a true original in rock and roll, with nobody before him sounding like he did and nobody later quite capturing his sound, despite attempts by artists like Captain Beefheart and Paul McCartney. "Nobody before him sounded like he did, and while many later tried, everyone from Captain Befart to Paul McCartney, nobody ever quite sounded like him later."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Uninspired First Specialty Session
podcast.body: Richard's initial recording session for Specialty Records at Cosimo Matassa's Studio, using Fats Domino's session musicians, was largely unsuccessful. Bumps Blackwell noted Richard's lack of energy in the studio compared to his live performances. "Blackwell had heard that Richard was an astounding live act, but he was just doing nothing in the studio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Weird and Scary Image
podcast.body: Little Richard was identified as another artist, alongside Billy Lee Riley, who pushed the boundaries of the then-radical world of rock and roll with a "weird and scary" persona. "And there were others like him, like the weird and scary little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Worry About "Devil Music"
podcast.body: As Richard's fame grew, so did his ego, but he also started to express concern about whether he should be creating what he perceived as "devil music," hinting at the future conflict between his religious beliefs and rock and roll career. "But Richard was also becoming a big star himself, and he was getting an ego to go along with it, and he was starting to worry whether he should be making this devil music at all."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Toronto Rock and Roll Revival Performance (September 13, 1969)
xref.body: John Lennon performed at Varsity Stadium in Toronto, facing severe stage fright and heroin withdrawal, as it was his first performance outside The Beatles. He was also intimidated by other acts on the bill, including his idols Chuck Berry, Gene Vincent, and Little Richard. "This was the first time John had ever performed outside the Beatles, which at the time were still a going concern."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Godmother of Rock and Roll"
xref.body: Her profound and intense influence on foundational rock and roll figures such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis, and Jerry Lee Lewis earned her the prestigious title of "Godmother of Rock and Roll." This recognition highlights her crucial role in shaping the nascent genre. "And her influence was so intense and so profound on people like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis and Jerry Lee Lewis that she has been called the Godmother of Rock and Roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: African American Originator of Rock
xref.body: Ice-T often emphasized that rock music had its origins in African American artists, citing Chuck Berry as a prime example. "Ice Tea was always quick to point out that rock originated with African American artists like Chuck Berry and Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Closeted Queer Identity
xref.body: While Sister Rosetta Tharpe was queer, she maintained privacy about her sexuality. This detail is contrasted with Little Richard's more open, albeit conflicted, expression of his sexuality. "I mentioned that sister Rosetta was queer, but that was something that she kept quiet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career Struggles as David Jones
xref.body: Before adopting his famous stage name, David Bowie was known by his birth name, David Jones. He began his musical career under this name and initially struggled to make an impact. "It was pretty, you know, spacious Bowie or David Jones as he was known back then, which is his real name, tried real hard to make something happen with music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Music
xref.body: Jerry Lee Lewis's music was directly associated with the rock and roll sound of the 1950s and early 60s, which was a direct descendant of 12-bar blues. This music was characterized by clean, clear guitar sounds and mostly clean lyrics, often intended for kids and played on radio stations appealing to teenagers. "the rock and roll sound became associated and intertwined with the music of the 1950s and early 60s, Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was a foundational pioneer of rock and roll, counted among the "piano heroes" whose piano playing was central to the genre's initial sound. His style was key in shaping the percussive and energetic rhythm and blues-influenced foundation of early rock. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Fats Domino was an early pioneer in rock and roll, identified as one of the "piano heroes" whose instrument was fundamental to the genre's formation. His contributions helped integrate elements of jazz, boogie-woogie, and barrel house into the emerging rock sound. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Ray Charles was an early pioneer of rock and roll, considered one of the "piano heroes" who helped define the genre in its formative years. His piano style was instrumental in blending various musical influences, including jazz and rhythm and blues, into rock and roll. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Huey Piano Smith was an early pioneer of rock and roll, recognized as one of the "piano heroes" who shaped the genre's sound during its nascent stages. His energetic piano work contributed significantly to the "honkin rhythm" that was a hallmark of early rock and roll. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Pioneer
xref.body: Elvis contributed to the merge of R&B and several other genres that led to rock and roll in the 1950s. "Rock and Roll begins in the 1950s when R&B and several other genres merge, thanks to Elvis, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Pioneer
xref.body: Chuck Berry is cited as one of the major stars of the early rock and roll era, a romantic figure of legend who is well-documented in many books, in contrast to other important but lesser-known artists of the period. "While you won't find much out there on a lot of truly important artists, you can find out enough about Elvis and Ray Charles and Johnny Cash and Little Richard and Chuck Berry in the rest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.body: Vince Taylor, as part of the Playboys, was among the artists who followed Little Richard's flamboyant path, exhibiting a distinctive and fabulous style. "Vince Taylor in the playboys... They all sounded different, but they all had a specific sort of fabulous style about them."

xref.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a queer Black woman from Cotton Plant, Arkansas, is widely called the "Godmother of rock and roll." She was a pioneering guitarist who transitioned to the electric guitar, revered by figures like Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Chuck Berry for her influential bridge between gospel blues and swing music. "A lot of people will point to sister Rosetta Thar, a guitarist who graduated to the electric guitar and has been called the Godmother of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact on Rock's Unstoppable Rise
xref.body: The emergence of The Beatles, following Elvis, Little Richard, and Jerry Lee Lewis, cemented rock's status as an unstoppable force. Their success ensured that, despite criticisms from ministers, record burnings, and crackdowns by authorities, rock music would endure. "And then after the Beatles, rock was unstoppable. No matter how many ministers wailed against it, no matter how many records were burned, no matter how many authorities tried to crack down on it, rock was here to stay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Love for Little Richard
xref.body: As a young saxophone player, David Jones was a big fan of Little Richard, whose music and persona pushed the boundaries of early rock and roll. "David Jones was a young saxophone player who loved Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Probable Bisexuality
xref.body: Similar to David Bowie, Lou Reed was likely bisexual. His public persona and lyrical content often suggested a fluid sexuality, which was reinforced by his marriage to a woman in 1973 combined with the explicit themes in his music. "Probably bisexual, just like Bowie, and Little Richard admitted to being something after all his early success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."
